data.title: Google acquires Wyoming data center site from AI infrastructure firm Crusoe
data.description:
Google has acquired Crusoe's data center site in southeast Wyoming, the AI infrastructure developer said on Friday, a day after the Alphabet unit announced a $17-billion investment in the project.

Here are some details:

  • Google announced the investment on Thursday to build its first data center in Wyoming, expanding its AI infrastructure despite growing political opposition to such projects in parts of the US

  • Crusoe said it has completed its involvement in the project's pre-development phase, which included site selection, government approvals and power strategy

  • The deal's financial terms were not disclosed

  • The campus was initially developed by Crusoe and Tallgrass Energy

  • Google on Thursday said it would build the facility in partnership with Tallgrass Energy, as well as Black Hills Energy, American Electric Power and Related Digital

  • Crusoe Chief Executive Chase Lochmiller said the company has more than 6 gigawatts of contracted capacity and over 40 gigawatts in its development pipeline

  • Crusoe added that it is developing another Google data center campus in Armstrong, which it announced earlier this year

data.title: Torrent Gold to Acquire Sunset Tungsten Project
data.description:
Vancouver, British Columbia--(Newsfile Corp. - November 6, 2026) - Torrent Gold Inc. (FSE: RV00) ("Torrent" or the "Company") is pleased to announce that it has entered into a membership interest purchase agreement (the "Purchase Agreement"), dated November 6th, 2026, with Lamina Minerals LLC and Belle Morgan Ltd. (together, the "Vendors"). Pursuant to the Purchase Agreement, the Company proposes to acquire a series of nineteen unpatented lode mining claims located in Hidalgo County, New Mexico and commonly known as the "Sunrise Tungsten Project" (together, the "Project").

In consideration for the Project, the Company has agreed to: (i) complete a cash payment of Cdn$100,000, (ii) issue 3,500,000 common shares (the "Consideration Shares") and, (iii) grant a one-and-one-half percent (1.5%) net smelter returns royalty (the "Royalty") on commercial production from the Project, to the Vendors. The Company will be entitled to purchase three-quarters-of-one percent (0.75%) of the Royalty, at any time within ten years of closing, for a one-time cash payment of US$1,000,000.

The Company is at arms-length from each of the Vendors. No finders' fees or commissions are payable by the Company in connection with completion of the transaction contemplated by the Purchase Agreement. The Consideration Shares will be subject to a statutory hold period of four months and one day from the date of issuance, in accordance with applicable Canadian securities laws and such other further restrictions as may apply under foreign securities laws.

The transaction contemplated by the Purchase Agreement will constitute a "major acquisition" for the Company, in accordance with the policies of the Canadian Securities Exchange, on the basis that it is expected to comprise the majority of the operating assets of the Company in the twelve month period following closing. As a result, completion of the transaction will be subject to the approval of the Canadian Securities Exchange. The transaction is not expected to result in a "Change of Control" for the Company, within the meaning prescribed by the policies of the Canadian Securities Exchange, nor is it expected to result in any changes to the board of directors or management of the Company,

About Torrent Gold Inc.

Torrent Gold is a mineral and natural resources exploration company that leverages its years of combined experience in capital markets and mining for acquisition and exploration during the resource commodity cycles.

data.title: Readers Remember Their Favorite Small Businesses — WSJ
data.description:
By Demetria Gallegos

My childhood neighborhood had two corner grocery stores within a few blocks of our home. I could go to either one with the quarters I had found under the sofa (and on my dad's dresser) and get some candy. A windfall might net me a mini fruit pie. And the independence of it was half the magic.

Today, children are more likely to have to go to a chain grocery store for candy, and odds are they'd have to be driven there, and escorted through the purchase by a reproving adult.

The kinds of small businesses and experiences that we cherished in the past are harder to find these days, and Wall Street Journal readers think something consequential has been lost.

We asked them, "Tell us about small businesses you remember fondly. What do you miss most about them?" Here are some of their answers. And a few of the beloved places that are still holding on.

Yearning for a plain old sandwich

I remember seeing independent sandwich shops everywhere. These weren't gourmet sandwiches or full-scale delis by any stretch of the imagination, but were places that you could get a good sandwich basket with chips, maybe some soup, and enjoy an affordable lunch at a nonchain restaurant.

Sure, New York City and Chicago still have many such places that also double as classic delis. But in my hometown of Kansas City, all the sandwich shops are now chain locations or have upscaled to something beyond a routine sandwich by offering organic/farm-fresh (read: expensive) odd takes on traditional sandwiches. What happened to these places? — Dillon Evans, Kansas City, Mo.

Know-it-alls (in a good way)

My father worked as a salesman for over 35 years at the original Black & Company Hardware Store on N. Water Street in Decatur, Ill., beginning in 1944. While the business is still in operation as an industrial and safety equipment supplier and has expanded to other cities, then it was a classic local hardware store, composed of two large rooms.

One room had squeaky, thin-slat wooden floors that housed a small department store assortment of dishes, kitchen appliances, tools, fans — just about anything a house would need. Shelves were packed with goods but well organized. A high shelf containing larger items ringed the room and was accessible only by a ladder. The other larger room contained building supplies including lumber, and large bins filled with commonly used nails, etc., as well as bins containing various types of seeds.

What stood out was the knowledge base of the clerks. My father and the others could give a dissertation on different types of screws: steel, stainless steel, iron, aluminum, thread angles and thickness, and on and on. It was a small work family of men and women who stayed on the job for years, worked as a team and tried to provide excellent service. If someone walked in the door one minute before closing, they were still provided with the same service even if it took half an hour.

My father was very outgoing and wherever we went in town, he would meet and chat with Black's regular customers. We had to allow at least an extra 15 minutes to get from our parking spot to wherever we wanted to go if we needed to be on time. Even after my father retired, he was warmly greeted by former customers for the remainder of his life. — Mark Ridlen, Wakefield, R.I.

My world in two blocks

Growing up in the Logan neighborhood of Philadelphia there was a group of food stores two blocks from my home. The seafood store had a table with raised sides and carp swimming in it. Next to it was a dairy store where cream cheese was cut from large slabs. The bread store was next to the bakery, and the butcher shop's floor was thick with sawdust.

In the middle of the block was Ulitsky's Deli, which had pickle barrels and every deli food in the world. There were two hair salons, a dress shop and a pharmacy. I loved being there, walking from store to store. It's still vivid, and I'm 98. — Edward Jawer, Wyncote, Pa.

Their name on the door

The small businesses of my suburban childhood in Summit, N.J., are still vivid in my mind. Each was run by its namesake: Scotti's Record Shop, where Mr. Scotti sold me my first record, "Heartbreak Hotel." Louvis's Luncheonette, the place we would all congregate for vanilla Cokes after school, until Mr. Louvis kicked us out. Rogers Pharmacy — he knew us all by first names and the meds we needed.

What strikes me now is that the founders of these beloved small businesses not only ran their own shops. It was not only that they knew everyone in town, although that gave us a comfort level you simply cannot find at the supermarket checkout counter, even though the clerk "knows" you. These beloved shops were an extension of the owners themselves. If they closed, we were devastated, as if we'd lost a family member. — Ellen Geiger, Andover, Mass.

Graphic memory

There was a comic-book store named Copacetic Comics in Pittsburgh, in the Polish Hill neighborhood, that was up two (very narrow) flights of stairs. It specialized in graphic novels from independent publishers and the gentleman who ran it gave a strong impression of having read everything in the store. You would pick up a book, and he would explain how the author had taken five years to paint all of the images in it.

I always felt so lucky to have a store like that in my city because of the unique, deep knowledge of the owner and the thoughtful selection of what was on display in the tiny store. — Mary E. Carter, Pittsburgh

Cheap, good eats

I miss the buffets on Fremont Street in Vegas in the 1970s. I used to go there for trade shows. I'd take a run in the early morning, then hit the buffet, with time to spare to get to our booth. I used to love showing that $2.95 buffet receipt to my company on my expense report.

The buffets were wonderful — much better than any hotel restaurant I ever stayed in. That they were cheaper was a bonus. Close, cheap, good. What's not to like? You didn't have to be a guest. They were open to the public.

Honestly, it was all of an era with regular visitors getting rooms "comped," and waitresses bringing drinks on the house if you sat at a slot long enough. Two-dollar blackjack tables. Nickel slots. Free parking. A weekend in Las Vegas could cost little more than what you left behind in the casino, and your casino chip was currency all over town. — Mike Knudsen, Trabuco Canyon, Calif.

I still remember the smell

Perhaps the most iconic small business in my hometown of Arlington, Va., was Ayers Hardware, which announced in July that it would be shutting its doors after almost 80 years. When I went to the Arlington Reddit to commiserate with my fellow Arlingtonians, the commenters read my mind. I immediately spotted a reply saying the user could practically smell the place just by seeing a picture.

When I was a kid, my friends and I would go in with a few dollars of cash and be able to buy tons of candy, some of which was so "vintage" it was impossible to find elsewhere. The place had a relaxed vibe with friendly employees, and I'd say what I miss most is that it didn't feel "optimized."

I find newer stores are sterile, cheaply designed efficiency factories to get customers in and out at record pace, where patrons could go 10 trips without speaking to another person. Perhaps those kinds of stores are more profitable and thus will beat out small businesses in the long run, but it leaves you missing something. — Jack Fisher, Arlington, Va.

Anchor store

I miss the 5 & 10. It was just this eclectic little store that had a bit of everything. As a kid, it was a rite of passage to be old enough to walk to the 5 & 10 to get some type of random candy — Razzles for me, why I have no idea — and to browse the makeup I hoped to someday be old enough to wear.

Once that store departed from Bedford Avenue in my small hometown of Bellmore, N.Y., it seemed it wasn't long before all the mainstays that had been there from the beginning were gone soon after (including the grocery store that burned down, the bakery, and the men's clothing store where my grandfather bought his fedoras). — Melissa Mauro Hineman, Charleston, S.C.

No more house calls

I miss the nostalgia of the milk man delivering glass gallon jugs to our home in open wooden crates, and how we'd leave the old glass jugs out for him to recycle.

Also, the knife sharpener and floor polisher who made house calls. Most of all, I miss our family doctor who came to our home and who knew us all by name, along with our medical history, without having to look at his chart. — Leslie Price, Rockville Centre, N.Y.

Another milk memory

I remember drive-through dairies near our home in Fontana, Calif. They mostly sold milk products, but I seem to recall free Popsicles for the kids in the car. We could also ride our bikes to one near our house, and pick up the milk. Our single mom worked, so this was probably a help to her. — Patty Smith, San Luis Obispo, Calif.

Side hustle

I miss the corner candy store or luncheonettes of my early life in Brooklyn and Long Island. They had soda fountains, a grill, newspapers, magazines, stationery, toys, playing cards and some necessities. These stores also had at least two pay phones.

I spent a lot of birthday money and allowance buying small chess sets, Spaulding balls and malteds at these establishments.

Later on, I learned that some of the proprietors also had a sideline...taking bets. — Charles-Eric Gordon, Plainview, N.Y.

data.title: Alpha Cognition to Participate in Upcoming Investor Events
data.description:
Alpha Cognition Inc. () (“Alpha Cognition”, or the “Company”), a biopharmaceutical company developing and commercializing novel therapeutics for debilitating neurodegenerative disorders, today announced that Michael McFadden, Chief Executive Officer, and Lauren D’Angelo, Chief Operating Officer, will participate in the upcoming investor events:

Craig-Hallum Alpha Select Conference
Format: 1x1 meetings

Date: Tuesday, November 17, 2026

Stonegate CEO Series
Format: Fireside chat

Date/Time: Thursday, December 10, 2026 at 12pm EST

For further information regarding these events, please reach out to your institutional representative.

About Alpha Cognition Inc.

Alpha Cognition Inc. is a commercial stage, biopharmaceutical company dedicated to developing treatments for patients with neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer’s disease and Cognitive Impairment with mild Traumatic Brain Injury (“mTBI”), for which there are limited or no approved treatment options.

ZUNVEYL is a patented drug approved as a new generation acetylcholinesterase inhibitor for the treatment of Alzheimer’s disease, with expected minimal gastrointestinal side effects. ZUNVEYL’s active metabolite is differentiated from donepezil and rivastigmine in that it binds neuronal nicotinic receptors, most notably the alpha-7 subtype, which is known to have a positive effect on cognition. ALPHA-1062 is also being developed in combination with memantine to treat moderate to severe Alzheimer’s dementia, and as an intranasal formulation for Cognitive Impairment with mTBI.

data.title: Crude Oil Advances As U.S.-Iran War Concerns Continue While Qatar Steps Up Mediation Efforts
data.description:
WASHINGTON (dpa-AFX) - Recovering from earlier losses in the session, crude oil prices have moved higher on Friday as signals of war risk continued after U.S. President Donald Trump refused to rule out renewing attacks on Iran. This overshadowed the positivity from reports hinting that Qatar is speeding up the efforts to clear way for U.S.-Iran peace process.

WTI Crude Oil for December delivery was last seen trading up by $0.46 (or 0.51%) at $90.98 per barrel

Investors are yet to receive clarity on how the U.S. administration plans to defuse the Middle East crisis and figure out a way to permanently end all hostilities with Iran.

Trump suffered a setback this week when the midterm election results showed that the Democratic party seized control of the House and Senate.

While Trump remarked that Iran was partly responsible for the jolt, U.S. Vice President JD Vance conceded that Iran war was the primary reason for the defeat.

The war with Iran, which began in late February and is in its ninth month now, has rattled energy markets around the world after Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz.

Prior to the elections, reports indicated a possible renewal of attacks on Iran by the U.S. on a grand scale after the elections.

Defiant Iran responded by stating that Iran could combat any attack by any aggressor and would strike back, ignoring geographical boundaries.

However, the results indicated that public support shifted in favor of the Democrats as U.S. households could not bear the squeezing on their budgets due to oil-linked inflation as a consequence of the U.S.-Iran war that Trump started.

Despite conquering Congress, the Democrat-elects have to wait until January to assume office. This period offers more than 60 days for Trump to either carry out the attacks as planned or attempt to solve the crisis through negotiations or as a third option enforce the current economic blockade for an extended period without ordering withdrawal of troops.

Yesterday, Trump stated that the world will soon know his decision on the possibility of a deal with Iran. Declining to rule out military option, Trump maintained that he could destroy what is left of Iran.

Trump replaced White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller who was the Deputy Chief of Staff. Of note, in April, Miller remarked that if Iran refused a deal, the U.S. blockade could continue without an end. As a last resort, he also suggested the destruction of Iran's energy infrastructure.

Reuters reported, citing an Iranian official, that Iran had sent a nuclear proposal to the U.S. through Qatar, with a precondition that a discussion will not begin until Iran's conditions are met by the U.S.

While Iran wants the lifting of U.S. sanctions, release of frozen Iranian assets in foreign countries, and adequate compensation for war losses, the U.S. wants a halt to Iran's nuclear program.

Today, Qatar officially stated that the Emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani had a discussion with Trump over phone about de-escalation.

Causes of concern continue to remain as the Strait of Hormuz shipping traffic is still under threat.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations reported an explosion on an oil tanker on its port side, 16 nautical miles east of Khasab, Oman, in the Strait of Hormuz yesterday.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps announced that two oil tankers that tried to transit the Strait of Hormuz through unauthorized routes struck mines.

While one tanker was hit in the eastern part of the strait, the other was struck within the strait itself. Soon after hitting the mines, the vessels caught fire.

The IRGC re-asserted Iran's stance that the strait will remain closed until Iran's conditions are fully met.

Even while the uncertainty over the U.S. strategy to deal with Iran continued to add geopolitical risk premium and pushed oil prices higher, expectations on a possible diplomatic solution partly offset the fears.

Today's economic data in the U.S. revealed stronger-than-expected payroll numbers.

The U.S. dollar index was last seen trading at 102.28, up by 0.70 (or 0.69%) today.

data.title: Saudi National Accused of Bugging OpenAI's Office Pleads Not Guilty — WSJ
data.description:
By Maxwell Zeff

Abdulrahman Alfozan, the Saudi national accused of bugging a restricted OpenAI conference room, pleaded not guilty on Friday in a federal court in San Francisco.

Appearing before a U.S. magistrate judge for an arraignment hearing, Alfozan's lawyer, David W. Rizk, said his client would plead not guilty for the single count he has been charged with: intercepting oral communications. The maximum penalty for the charge is five years in prison and a fine of $250,000.

Alfozan is currently in federal custody, and is next scheduled to appear in court on Nov. 17.

Alfozan is accused of wrapping a thumb-sized circuit board and microphone in toilet paper and inserting the device behind a wall-mounted TV inside an executive conference room in OpenAI's office around Sept. 28, shortly before he was set to leave the country. The Saudi national had been an employee on OpenAI's product team since July 2025 until he was fired in October, the same day he was arrested and charged.

Prosecutors previously alleged Alfozan booked one-way plane tickets from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia via Istanbul for himself, his wife and their newborn son departing on Oct. 12. Alfozan's wife and son left without him shortly after his arrest, prosecutors said.

The wife and child's one-way plane tickets were initially paid for by the Saudi government, but that flight was canceled, prosecutors said. They were then rebooked on another one-way flight to Qatar, this time in business class, by a member of the Saudi military, the filing said.

Lawyers representing Alfozan said the military official was the brother-in-law of his wife, and that she left because of issues with her visa. Alfozan's lawyers previously said she planned to return to the U.S. to support her husband.

Write to Maxwell Zeff at maxwell.zeff@wsj.com

data.title: Canada Fiscal, Rate Policies Look to Be Working at Cross Purposes — Market Talk
data.description: Canadian fiscal and monetary policies could be working at cross purposes, the chief economist at BMO Capital Markets tells clients in his week-ending note. Douglas Porter says the annual Canadian government budget plan is "meatier" than expected and delivers a significant dollop of fiscal stimulus — so much so that BMO has upgraded its Canada GDP growth forecast in 2027 to 2% from 1.8%. Meanwhile, the Bank of Canada raised rates to deal with an elevated inflation forecast, and could hike again. "If that's not rowing in different directions, it's not at all obvious what would count as policy friction," Porter says. In addition, he adds, weak jobs data, a pullback in oil prices and the tech selloff could prompt BOC policymakers to reconsider whether another hike in December is required. (paul.vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

data.title: Cross-Border Payments Firm Behneh Files for IPO
data.description:
By Katherine Hamilton

Behneh filed for an initial public offering.

The Singapore-based financial technology company plans to offer 5 million shares for $3 to $5 apiece.

It intends to trade on Nasdaq under the ticker BENE.

Behneh offers cross-border payments to retail and institutional clients, including collection on behalf and payment on behalf services.

Its core business facilitates international transfers and related payment processing services. In addition to remittances, Behneh has more recently expanded into providing advisory services.

Following a 2023 inspection, deficiencies were identified in Behneh's money laundering and terrorism defense controls. Issues included customer due diligence and wire-transfer compliance.

Behneh said it has since implemented remediation measures to strengthen its security and compliance measures.

In the six months ended April 30, 2026, one customer accounted for 85% of Behneh's revenue. Total revenue during that time increased 17% to $504,893, compared with the same period the year before.

Write to Katherine Hamilton at katherine.hamilton@wsj.com

data.title: The AI Crash Broke the Market. Here Are 3 Things That Decide What's Next. — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Martin Baccardax

Aristotle never said "nature abhors a vacuum," but his insistence that empty space must always be filled created the rule that Wall Street lives by.

The stock market, by the way, hates the rule but follows it anyway, filling up the blank days on economic calendars, the weekends, and the holidays with all sorts of theories, rumors, and wagers — many that send investors in the wrong direction.

And that puts the market's end-of-year run, which includes 34 full trading days and trio of early closures, back in focus — especially after Tuesday's midterm elections triggered this brutal AI sell-off.

There are effectively only three calendar items left that will either steady investors' nerves or deepen their jitters: Nvidia's third-quarter earnings update, the planned public listing of AI start-up Anthropic, and the Federal Reserve's December rate decision. And there's one subject that has been a point of discussion for months now: the Iran war.

First, though a look at this past week to understand what's at stake going forward: The Nasdaq Composite fell into correction territory and had its biggest loss in market value on record. Plus, the AI trade is still facing its biggest test since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022.

For Alex Guiliano, of Resonate Wealth Partners, there certainly is uncertainty and a good possibility of more losses.

"This is a stock market that is trying to figure out the right valuations for the AI trade and grappling with a swift sentiment shift after the midterm elections," said Guiliano, Resonate Wealth's chief investment officer.

Before and after 2018's midterms, "the stock market experienced significant volatility and declined nearly 20%, so there is a historical precedent for more downside risk ahead," he added.

The next leg lower isn't hard to visualize: the Nasdaq is now less than 1% higher than it was at the end of July. The S&P 500 is sitting on a loss of 1.1% for the second half of the year.

Democratic wins in key states, including in Georgia, Texas, and Ohio, will probably put restrictions on AI data centers. And the blue wave on Capitol Hill could mean a regulation crackdown for the market's most-important sector.

And Wall Street's appetite for the AI trade, in the form of Anthropic's $1.5 trillion IPO, will no doubt be tested, too.

The S&P 500 Information Technology sector, in fact, is trading at the lowest levels in six months, and the Communications Services sector is at its lowest levels of the year. Together, the two make up half of the S&P 500's $67.4 trillion in market value.

Fourth-quarter earnings for both should still be solid and contribute 45.4% of the $810 billion in collective S&P 500 profits expected over the three months.

But tech's share of the profits is starting to slow and so is the overall rate for broader earnings growth. LSEG data shows overall profits will rise by 35% this year but fall by more than half — to 16% — in the coming year.

That's pretty much in line with what Capital Economics' John Higgins is expecting.

"We think there is plenty of scope for the rout [in both sectors] to continue in 2027 even if there is a rebound before the end of this year," he said.

"But we would be surprised if there were ultimately as big peak-to-trough drawdowns [in the tech and communications services sectors] as there were after the dotcom bubble burst," said Higgins, whose title is chief economic adviser.

"That's because this time the rally is more 'fundamental' than 'speculative,' judging by the relative contributing of earnings and the price that investors were willing to pay for them."

So back to the future: Nvidia's earnings are Nov. 17, Anthropic's IPO should come later this month, maybe before Thanksgiving, and the Fed's next policy meeting is Dec. 9. And the Iran war is in a holding pattern, for now.

Investors have to think about all of these things.

They even put the chances of an escalation in war behind them, either, even with last week's 14% slide in Brent crude prices, the largest in more than six years.

Nor can they discount the impact oil will have on inflation readings and, by extension, the Fed's final rate decision of the year.

Which, for ING economist James Smith, may now be cast in a very different light because of how the central bank's chairman, Kevin Warsh, is thinking.

"The rout in AI stocks matters because Warsh has rationalized a decent chunk of the Fed's rate hikes through loose financial conditions, widely seen as a euphemism for soaring equity prices," he said. "That's clearly changing. And a much deeper correction could raise serious doubts about another December hike."

Friday's strong jobs report, however, has kept the rate-hike heat at a simmer. The odds of a quarter-point increase, which would take the target to 4%-nd 4.25%, now stand at 80%, according to the CME FedWatch.

But, as Hirtle & Co.'s Brad Conger points out, the jobs report and the Fed projections are running a distant second to the market's AI trade — and there are few, if any, answers as to where that's headed.

"Under normal circumstances, an unexpectedly strong jobs report would crush Treasuries and lift rate hike expectations, but given the rout in the AI capex sectors over the past couple of weeks, all data points will be considered extremely 'backward looking'.

"All eyes are, rightly, are on the semiconductor stocks and the Anthropic IPO," said Cooper, who is Hirtle's chief investment officer.

In other words, chips and one very big public debut are what will fill the empty space.

November is historically the market's strongest month, with an average gain of 1.9% and upside moves 70% of the time since 1950, according to the Stock Trader's Almanac.

Maybe that will calm those late-autumn jitters, maybe not. But investors could use history repeating itself right about now.

Write to Martin Baccardax at martin.baccardax@barrons.com
